title: Losing Is Information
part: PART ONE: EIGHT GAMES, ZERO WINS

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #10: Ask the scoreboard how you're doing.*

The bus engine cuts off, and the air inside is still thick with the smell of wet wool and old rubber. I stand up, my knees cracking a little, because I am twelve and I am angry.

"You said that was data," I say. My voice shakes, but I hold it steady. "It’s not. It’s losing. We lost eight games. That is not information. That is a fact. A bad fact."

Gin doesn’t look up from her thermos. She unscrews the cap, and the smell hits me first: black tea, strong enough to strip paint. She pours a cup, and the liquid is dark, almost brown, sloshing against the plastic rim.

"The scoreboard tells you what happened," she says. Her voice is low. It is the voice of someone who has driven six hours in the rain and seen a deer jump the median. "It does not tell you who you are. Those are two different maps, Dani. You are looking at the wrong one."

I cross my arms. I want to say that maps are just facts too. I want to say that losing means the map is wrong. But she is already drinking, and the steam from the cup fogs the glass, hiding her face.
pages.image: A wiry girl with a yellow armband and high ponytail stands angrily in a big blank yellow minibus aisle; an older woman in a yellow windbreaker sits calmly, holding a steaming plastic cup of dark tea; hard yellow seats surround them.

pages.text:
"That is easy for you to say," I snap. "You are not the one standing in the mud while the whole school watches you fail. You just drive a bus."

Gin sets the cup down with a soft thud. She taps the screen above the driver’s seat, and the video pauses on the moment before the own goal. My face is frozen in a grimace, looking like a deer that has realized it is about to be a statistic.

"I care about winning," she says, her voice flat and steady. "I care more than you know. But I do not think it is the only thing worth measuring. Tell me. In that game, what did you do well?"

I open my mouth, then close it again. My brain scrambles through the highlights, searching for a save or a nice pass, but it only finds the noise, the whistles, and the laughter echoing in my ears.

"Nothing," I whisper, the word tasting like old pennies.

Gin nods slowly. She does not look disappointed, or even surprised. She looks like she is waiting for me to finish a sentence I have not yet started, her eyes steady and unblinking. She reaches into her pocket and pulls out a small, worn whistle. It is silver and dented, looking like it has survived a lot of things.

"Then we start there," she says, tapping the metal against her thumb. "Find the one thing. Just one."
pages.image: A close-up of a dented silver whistle held in a wrinkled hand; in the background, a small TV screen displays a paused video of a girl in a red jersey looking down in shame.

pages.text:
The Dugout Diner is where time goes to hide, and the milkshakes taste like cold metal mixed with regret. We sit in the corner booth as a lump of red jerseys, elbows touching, knees knocking, while the sticky floor grabs at our shoes like it has a personal grudge against us.

Tank picks at a single french fry. He looks at his plate, then at me. "I think I can stop the winger," he says quietly. His voice is soft, like a dog breathing. "If I stop apologizing first. The apologies make me slow. Sorry, sorry, sorry. It’s a habit. I am working on it."

Josie shakes her leg without stopping. "The coach is weird," she says. "She watches us like we are ants in a jar. I like ants. But she is weird."

Ahmed slurps his shake, making a loud, wet noise that echoes off the tile. "The coach is weird," he agrees. "And also wrong. Passing is slow. She wants us to pass. It is illogical."

The twins finish each other’s sentence in perfect sync. "Weird in stereo," Leo says.

"Weird in stereo," Mateo repeats.

I look at my own shake. The foam is settling into a flat, gray circle that looks exactly like the puddle of glue I spilled on my math homework last Tuesday.
pages.image: A group of young soccer players in red jerseys sit in a diner booth; a large boy picks at a fry, a fast boy slurps a shake, and two identical boys look at the table; the floor is shiny and sticky.

pages.text:
I am back at the bus. The rain has stopped, but the air is heavy. I take the yellow armband off my left arm. It feels lighter than it should. It feels like taking off a weight that was never mine to carry.

I place it on the seat next to Gin’s thermos. The yellow fabric looks bright against the dull yellow plastic. It looks like a wound.

"I’m not the right captain," I say. My voice is flat. "For a team that doesn’t care about winning. If you don’t care about the scoreboard, I don’t know who I am. I am just Dani. And Dani is bad at soccer."

Gin looks at the armband. She does not move to take it. She looks at me for a long time. Her eyes are behind her sunglasses, so I cannot see them.

"Give me a week," she says. She reaches out and pushes the armband back toward me with one finger. It slides across the plastic. "If it is still no, we will both quit. But not today. Today, we are just wet."
pages.image: A yellow armband lies on a yellow plastic big blank yellow minibus seat next to a steel thermos; an older woman’s finger pushes the armband back toward a girl who is watching with a serious face; rain streaks the window behind them.

pages.text:
Abuela’s car is slow. It moves through the wet streets like a turtle dragging a shell. I watch the world go by, the houses blurring into gray shapes. The windows are fogged up. I press my nose against the glass. The smell of the inside of the car is old bread and pine cleaner.

We pass the duck pond. The water is black and still. A duck is sitting on my ball. It is my ball, the one I kicked over the crossbar last week, and the duck is sitting on it at the water's edge like it paid for it.

I watch it. It does not move. It looks at me. It does not give it back.

I take out the red notebook. The pages are soft from my hands. I turn to a blank page. My hand hovers over the paper. I have written so many ways to lose. But I have never written a way to win. Or a way to stay.

I write: *Priya stayed in the goal.*

It is small. It is quiet. But it is true.
pages.image: A girl in a car looks out a fogged window at a dark pond; a duck sits on a soccer ball at the water's edge; the girl holds a red notebook in her lap, her hand poised to write.
